items.title: Aluminium 'wants' to react but doesn't
items.claim: Aluminium has a standard electrode potential of minus 1.66 V — more reactive than zinc or iron. It should fizz in water and burn in air. Yet aluminium aircraft, foil and cans sit happily for years.
items.prompt: Why doesn't aluminium corrode in air?

options.text: Pure aluminium does not react with oxygen
Aluminium instantly forms a coherent, impermeable 4 nanometre oxide layer (Al2O3) that protects the metal underneath
The factory coats aluminium with plastic before sale
Standard electrode potentials are unreliable for s and p block metals

items.reveal_title: Thermodynamics screams react! — but a passivation layer locks the door
items.reveal:
Aluminium oxide forms in milliseconds when fresh aluminium meets oxygen. Unlike iron oxide (rust), Al2O3 has almost the same molar volume as the underlying metal, so it forms a tight, adherent film. Oxygen can't reach the metal beneath, and the reaction effectively stops.

Remove the oxide (scratch it, dissolve it in alkali, or amalgamate the surface with mercury), and aluminium reacts violently. This is why aluminium powder + iron oxide (thermite) is dangerous, and why aluminium ships are vulnerable to mercury contamination.
items.why: Reactivity series is about thermodynamic tendency. Kinetics — including passivation — decides whether the reaction is observable.

items.title: Mass spec can distinguish CO from N2 — molecules differing by 0.004 atomic mass units
items.claim: Carbon monoxide has exact mass 28.0101 u. Nitrogen gas has exact mass 28.0061 u. A high-resolution mass spectrometer can tell them apart routinely. Modern Orbitrap and FT-ICR instruments achieve resolutions of 1 part in 100,000 or better.

options.text: By weighing on a very sensitive scale

By measuring the frequency at which ions orbit in a magnetic or electrostatic trap; ion frequency is a precise function of mass-to-charge, and modern electronics measure frequencies to extraordinary precision
By averaging millions of low-resolution scans

items.reveal:
In an FT-ICR mass spectrometer, ions trapped in a magnetic field B orbit at the cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm). The image current induced in detection plates is recorded and Fourier-transformed to give the mass spectrum.

Frequency can be measured to about 1 part in 10 to the 9; mass-to-charge can be determined to about 1 part in 10 to the 6 with a well-calibrated instrument.

This is why high-resolution mass spec can identify peptides by exact mass alone, distinguish isotope clusters in metabolites, and resolve overlapping signals in complex mixtures. Proteomics, drug metabolism, environmental analysis and forensics all rely on it.

The 0.004 u difference between CO and N2 comes from the slightly different nuclear binding energies of the constituent nuclei — mass spec is sensitive enough to probe nuclear physics from chemistry samples.
items.why: Mass spec sounds like 'a scale for molecules'. It is really a precision frequency measurement of trapped ions in fields.

items.title: The modern atomic theory began with a colour-blind Quaker schoolmaster
items.claim: In 1803-1808 John Dalton, a Quaker schoolteacher in Manchester with no university post, proposed that elements are made of indivisible atoms with fixed mass. Compounds form by simple integer ratios of atoms. His theory still underpins everything in chemistry.
items.prompt: What evidence convinced chemists Dalton was right?

options.text: He saw atoms with a microscope

The law of multiple proportions: when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios (e.g. carbon to oxygen is 1:1.33 in CO and 1:2.67 in CO2)

items.reveal_title: Whole-number ratios point to discrete particles
items.reveal:
Dalton noticed that elements combine in fixed proportions (Proust's law of definite proportions, 1799) and that when they form multiple compounds, the mass ratios are simple whole numbers.

For carbon and oxygen: in CO, 12 g C combines with 16 g O. In CO2, 12 g C combines with 32 g O. Ratio 16:32 = 1:2. Only discrete units (atoms) combining in integer numbers can produce such patterns.

Dalton was colour-blind — he wrote the first scientific description of the condition (now called Daltonism) and never knew sodium emits yellow light because he couldn't see yellow. He died in 1844 and his coffin was followed by 40,000 mourners in Manchester.
items.why: Foundational scientific theories often come from outsiders working without elite credentials. Dalton was a schoolmaster, not a professor.
